lines.note: Sogi/sogu denotes slicing or cutting off on the slant; the Portuguese describes an oblique cut directed forwards. The printed historical enuiaſado is retained rather than modernized.
The directional gloss ends here; hana and mimi identify the nose and ears as objects of cutting. The joined mimiuoſogu is kept as printed, and Cor- continues on the next row.
Completes Cortar and translates the example as cutting off noses and ears. This is the continuation of sogu, not another entry.
Bin wo sogu concerns trimming the hair at the temples. The pilcrow introducing this example is visible and was missing from the provisional text.

runs.text: das fontes mais curtos cortandoos, & torcendo

lines.note: The gloss specifies shortening the temple hair by cutting and twisting it. Fontes here means the temples; the final torcendo governs os on the following row.

Os por ornato completes the hair-trimming example. The parenthesized phrase at the right is physically displaced: it completes the following Soguigami definition, and is preserved at its printed position rather than joined to this sentence.
Sogigami names temple hair arranged in the manner just described. Concertados connects with the displaced desta maneira printed at the right of the preceding physical row.

runs.text: O arrancar os cabelos dos cantos, ou ẽ-

lines.note: This entry describes plucking hair from the corners or recesses of the forehead. The abbreviation tilde and the actual line-end division in ẽ- are retained.
Completes entradas da testa, explaining ornamental plucking at the forehead. Sogobitai then names the resulting forehead configuration; its caron agrees with the entry above.

runs.text: Teſta ſem os cabelos dambas as partes deſta

lines.note: Defines a forehead lacking hair on both sides in this fashion. Dambas is the printed contraction, not a reason to add a modern word boundary.
Maneira completes the description of the plucked forehead. The short continuation is a real physical body row and remains separate.

Sogo is disagreement or discrepancy, and sogoshita koto is something inconsistent. The Portuguese infinitive and following example distinguish this entry from the homograph about Buddhist sayings below.
Translates sogoshita koto as a discrepant thing or matter. The complete short gloss belongs to the preceding example.

runs.text: Sentença dos que ſe ſeguirão depois de

lines.note: The second Sogo concerns sayings of those who followed Shaka. The printed seguirão is preserved in its historical context rather than silently changed to a modern past-tense spelling.

Xaca completes the Portuguese explanation with Shaka's name; Sogo and Butgo contrast ancestral or patriarchal sayings with Buddha's words. The name is printed in the italic explanation, while the Japanese example is upright.
Sogo is bodily appearance or physiognomy, paraphrased with katachi. Both carons are visible; the Portuguese filoſomia is retained as printed rather than replaced with a modern spelling.
Completes the physiognomy gloss by specifying the face. The inherited short-s transcription in rosto is retained; the st ligature is not globally normalized.
Sogo or soko is identified only as a particular medicine. The alternative marker is Latin l; the scan supports carons on both forms, without warrant for a more precise pharmacological identification.
Sogoi/sogoo means fitting or agreeing with someone. The past principal part visibly has a circumflex, ôta, rather than the provisional caron; this also agrees with the supplied NINJAL lexical entry.
Hito ni sogowanu mono is a person who does not fit or agree with others. The upright u and the negative ending explain the phrase; the Portuguese relative clause continues below.

runs.text: quadra, nem combina com os outros.

lines.note: Completes the description of someone incompatible with others. Both Portuguese verbs express agreement or suitability rather than a geometric square.

A regional variant of the preceding verb is assigned to Cami. Enlargement resolves Sogvi and the negative soguu-wanu sequence, not the malformed provisional Sogyi/soguu-iwanu; the supplied NINJAL entry corroborates the lexical reading, not the typography.

runs.text: Hũ peixe grãde como pargo do mar.

lines.note: Sogi names a large fish compared with a sea bream. The tildes in Hũ and grãde are visible; no exact modern species is imposed on this comparison.
This physical row was omitted from the provisional page. Sooji is explained as chi wo harau, sweeping the ground, and translated by cleaning and sweeping; it introduces the example on the next row.
Zashiki wo sooji suru is sweeping the room. The final Zaxiqui occurs inside the Portuguese translation and is wholly italic here, not the provisional mixture of an upright Z with italic remainder.
This homograph means possessing everything, paraphrased sube motsu. Its circumflex distinguishes it graphically from the cleaning entry; final upright S is the written-register label.

runs.text: Todo o exercito, ou todos os eſquadroẽs

lines.note: Soojin denotes the entire army or all its formations. The printed tilde falls in eſquadroẽs as shown, and the definition continues onto the next row.
Em universal completes the collective description of the army. The historical initial v in vniuerſal is preserved.
Soojuu, paraphrased soo no uchi, refers to everyone collectively. The final ẽ abbreviates em and is not an incomplete new word to expand in the canonical transcription.
Completes em commum, then introduces a decision made by all. The example's long-vowel marks and the Portuguese clause beginning He cousa are retained across the physical break.
Completes the statement that everyone agreed upon the matter. Assentar here is reaching a decision; its historical printed ending is not modernized.

Another omitted physical row introduces sooi, discrepancy, with the Japanese paraphrase aitagau. The example sooi-shita continues with koto on the next row; both printed hyphens and carons are preserved.

runs.text: Couſa que diſcrepa, ou he diferente.

lines.note: Koto completes the discrepancy example newly restored above. The gloss says the thing differs; the scan supports continuous diferente, not provisional di ſerente.

So-i is paraphrased soshin and defined as a careless or inattentive heart. The headword's hyphen and the following i marker replace OCR Soriri. The unusual Portuguese deſemoroſo is retained: enlargement favors e after ſ, though that vowel is weak, rather than silently regularizing the word to deſamoroſo.
Soi/soo describes being together with someone. The printed gloss is Estar junto de alguem, correcting the garbled provisional çunto ce while preserving the historical inflection and accents.
Kokoro mo mi ni sowanu describes being mentally beside oneself. The Portuguese comparison begins here and continues below; the damaged negative remains readable as souanu.
Completes the distracted-state gloss, then begins the maxim advising one to spend time with a person. The printed mi- continues as yo on the next row.

runs.text: yo, vmaniua notte miyo to yǔ.

lines.note: Completes miyo and contrasts knowing a person through companionship with knowing a horse by riding it. The Portuguese quereis is physically divided after que without a visible hyphen.

runs.text: reis conhecer o homẽ, estai cõ elle, & tratayo, &

lines.note: The translation says to stay with and associate with a man in order to know him. The crop shows elle and its preceding word space; homẽ and cõ retain their abbreviation marks.

runs.text: ſe quereis conhecer o cauallo, caualgai nelle.

lines.note: Finishes the maxim: to know the horse, ride it. The scan supports cauallo and nelle rather than the provisional couallo and nele; historical u/v usage remains unchanged.
Soiyoi hito is a person pleasant to be with. The Portuguese begins the positive description, completed by conversation on the next row.

After completing the pleasant-company gloss, soi noki no suru hito introduces someone whose acquaintance increasingly repels others. The following explanation and the cross-reference Soinoqino support noqino, not OCR ncqino.

runs.text: Homem que quanto mais o tratão, ou conuerſão

lines.note: Begins the description of a man whom people find less agreeable the more they associate or converse with him. The clause's consequence appears on the following row.

runs.text: faz por onde ſe apartem, & afastem delle.

lines.note: The man gives others cause to separate themselves and withdraw from him. This finishes the negative companionship example; the inherited st spelling in afastem is retained.
Soi yori no suru hito supplies the opposite case: a person who attracts closer acquaintance. Homem is divided without a visible terminal hyphen after ho.

runs.text: mẽ q̃ quãto mais ſe cõuerſa tanto mais atrahe.

lines.note: Completes the contrast: the more one converses with this person, the more he attracts. Atrahe is visible, not OCR atrabe; the multiple abbreviation tildes remain unexpanded.
Soihate means remaining with someone until death. The scan preserves the i in Soifate and the Portuguese Morrer sem se apartar, correcting the lost letters and fused words in the provisional reading.
Completes the definition as dying without separating from someone. This is the last physical body row of the left column, not a catchword.
This cross-reference points back to the soi entry and its example of companionship that drives people away. Vide is italic apparatus, while the referenced Japanese forms are upright.
Soitsume is a contemptuous designation for that person. The Portuguese is falando, speaking with contempt, not the provisional ſalando.
Soitoge means persevering in companionship with someone. The visible initial j in jũto restores the abbreviated Portuguese word that OCR reduced to ũto.
Completes the definition as not separating from that person. This follows the related expressions for remaining together in the other column.
Refers back to the soi entry's positive example of a person who attracts increasing intimacy. The whole referenced verb remains upright, including its final punctuation.
Soja or soja no koromo names a robe of thin fabric. Latin l introduces the alternative phrase; the Portuguese adjective delgada crosses the physical line break.

runs.text: gada como veo q̃ algũs Bõzos vestẽ porcima.

lines.note: The robe is veil-like and worn over other clothing by some Buddhist clergy. The abbreviations q̃, algũs, Bõzos, and vestẽ remain literal; the printed porcima is not respaced.
Sooja is described as the shrine with presiding authority, tsukasadoru yashiro. The Portuguese ermida is divided after er with no visible hyphen to supply.

runs.text: mida de Camis principal, & como matriz en-

lines.note: Continues the definition of a principal kami shrine, compared with a mother church. Camis is a Japanese-derived religious term embedded in the Portuguese explanation; entre begins at the right edge.
Completes entre as outras: the shrine is principal among the others. The short row is the end of the Sooja definition.
Soozen is paraphrased mado no mae, in front of the window. The final S is an upright written-register label rather than part of the italic gloss.

runs.text: Letra da China eſcrita de corrimão.

lines.note: Sooji denotes Chinese characters written in running or cursive hand. The final Portuguese word is read as corrimão; enlargement confirms the double r, while the last stroke of m is weak and can resemble n. The chosen reading is retained without replacing it with modern terminology.
Sojin denotes a common or ordinary person. The Portuguese cõmum contains an abbreviation tilde and is not silently expanded.

Soojite means generally or commonly. Second-pass enlargement shows an apparent n after õ and a visible separation at that point; the literal Cõ nummente is retained rather than normalized to Cõmummente. An incompletely printed initial m remains a nonblocking alternative.
Soojoo names a rank among Buddhist clergy. The gloss does not define the rank more narrowly; the headword's circumflex and caron are independently retained.

Soojuu is a running animal, and qedamono clearly supplies beast. The first paraphrase word appears to print Vaxiru, although the sense calls for hashiru; this anomalous initial is retained rather than silently emended to Faxiru.

runs.text: Serrador, ou o que corta, & faz ma-

lines.note: Soma denotes a sawyer or woodcutter. The Portuguese identifies the worker who cuts and prepares timber, with madeira divided after ma-.
Completes madeira no mato, timber prepared in the woods. This is the end of the woodcutter definition.

Somabito gives the same woodcutter meaning; its medial a is abraded but supported by the surviving word and supplied NINJAL entry. The right-hand no mato is displaced continuation of the next definition, not part of Idem.

runs.text: O ſerrar, cortar, ou fazer madeira

lines.note: Somadori names the activity of sawing, cutting, or preparing timber. Its final qualification no mato is printed at the far right of the preceding row and remains there in the transcription.
Somagi, paraphrased zaimoku, is timber not yet worked. The headword's worn letters read Somagui, corroborated by the supplied NINJAL index; per laurar retains the visible historical spelling.
The timber is just as it comes from the woods. This completes the contrast between raw wood and dressed timber.
Somari/somaru means becoming dyed, stained, or bathed in something. The following literal and figurative examples both depend on this intransitive sense.
Chi ni somaru means being stained or bathed in blood. The complete tingirſe is visible, correcting the omitted letter in provisional tingrſe; its complement follows below.
Completes sangue, then marks a figurative example: shoaku ni somaru, becoming steeped in evils. Permet. remains the printed apparatus abbreviation and is not expanded in the text.

runs.text: Eſtar inficionado de todas as maldades.

lines.note: Translates the figurative example as being infected by every kind of wickedness. Inficionado is the source's wording, not a modernization to another Portuguese verb.

runs.text: Somat. l, ſomatna. i, Socotnaru coto.

lines.note: Somat/somatna describes a careless or ill-made thing, paraphrased sokotsu naru koto with the dictionary's checked-t notation. The opening Cou- belongs to the italic Portuguese gloss, not Japanese text.
Completes cousa mal feita e desatentada, then starts an example of an exceptionally careless person. Somat carries into the next physical row without an added hyphen.
Daichino fitode gozaru completes the description of a very careless person. The crop reads daichino rather than OCR darichino and begins the Portuguese atabalhoado across the line break.
Completes atabalhoado and adds very inconsiderate. The visible mui corrects OCR mur; Somatna then begins a second adjectival example.
Mono completes somatna mono, an inattentive person. Somatni is then labelled an adverb; the tilde-bearing Portuguese deſatẽtado is retained without expansion.
Some/somuru is the transitive verb to dye. The scan clearly reads uru, not provisional urtu, and the example isho wo somuru concerns dyeing clothing.
Completes dyeing the garment, then begins fude wo somuru, literally dipping or staining the writing brush. The divided Japanese so- is wholly upright, correcting the provisional mixed-font fragment.
Finishes the brush expression and glosses it as writing, with an upright S register label. Somemono then introduces a dyed article as a separate illustrative form.
Defines somemono as something dyed, then introduces the auxiliary use of some/somuru. The final Iũ- begins junto on the next row; the provisional extra s has no support in the crop.

runs.text: to as raizes de outros verbos quer dizer, co-

lines.note: The verb, when joined to other verb stems, means to begin. Both junto and começar are divided across the surrounding physical rows and are not editorially rejoined.
Completes começar and gives omoi somuru, beginning to love or become attached. Initial V in Vomoi belongs to historical Japanese romanization, not a separate consonant to modernize.
Completes the example as beginning to love. The visible amar resolves the malformed provisional ariar and agrees with omoi somuru.
Soomei is perceptiveness, paraphrased by sharp hearing and clarity. The Portuguese begins hearing and penetrating matters, with penetrar divided after pe-.

runs.text: netrar bem, & com bom juizo as couſas.

lines.note: Completes the definition as understanding matters well and with good judgment. It explains intellectual discernment rather than hearing acuity alone.
Soomeidono denotes an official compared with a judge who hears cases. The duties continue on the following physical row.

Dispatching legal claims completes the official's duties. The parenthesized bem at the far right instead completes the following Soomeina definition and is retained as displaced text in its physical position.

runs.text: Peßoa q̃ ouue, & diſcerne, ou julga

lines.note: Soomeina describes a person who hears, discerns, or judges well. The adjective's ina ending is visible, correcting Sômema; its final bem is printed at the right of the preceding row.
Soomeini is the adverb corresponding to the discerning adjective. The grammatical abbreviation Adu. is italic apparatus, not part of the Japanese form.
Someiro is the colour of a dyed object. The entry returns from discernment vocabulary to the dyeing family.
Soomen is glossed by letria, fine noodles or vermicelli. The caron belongs to the Japanese headword and is retained distinctly from the circumflexes above.

runs.text: Caſa onde vendem, ou fazem a

lines.note: Soomenya is a place where the noodles are sold or made. The worn nya ending and final article a are recovered from the scan; the definition continues on the bottom row.

This bottom-left fragment completes the Soomenya definition and is body text, not a catchword. The provisional combined furniture record is split so the separate Someqi catchword is not swallowed into the definition.
The right-aligned catchword anticipates Someqi at the start of f445. It is separated from the body continuation letria on the same baseline and retains upright type.
